metadata.title: Internal Developer Platform Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how the internal developer platform would need to change after an acquisition, widespread use of coding agents, sovereignty rules, unsupported runtimes, customer-hosted deployment, or strong competition from packaged platforms.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: A developer selects a golden template, creates a repository, runs the standard delivery pipeline, provisions the company's preferred cloud and runtime, deploys a service, and observes it through shared tooling.
metadata.residualArchitecture: Instead of tying the developer experience to one template, cloud, runtime, pipeline, and human actor, the adapted design begins with a versioned service specification that says what a workload needs and who owns it. Provider adapters implement that specification on different stacks, policy checks both human- and agent-made changes, and evidence shows which capabilities and controls are satisfied. Acquisitions, sovereignty rules, exceptions, customer-hosted targets, and tool replacement can then be handled without rebuilding the whole platform.
metadata.note: The stressors are organizational, regulatory, customer, and market changes around software delivery. A broken pipeline by itself belongs in a failure drill, not in this list.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: An acquired business must remain on a different cloud and delivery stack for three years
stressors.detection: Acquisition due diligence, application inventory, cloud contracts, migration constraints, control assessments, and integration planning.
stressors.attractor: The internal platform is no longer one paved implementation road; forcing immediate migration blocks product integration, while accepting the acquired stack as an exception creates a permanent second platform.
stressors.businessReaction: Establish a common service and control contract, federate the acquired capabilities, make gaps visible, prioritize only valuable convergence, and give teams one discovery and support experience.
stressors.residue: Separate the service specification and platform capability model from provider implementation. Cloud, runtime, pipeline, registry, identity, and observability adapters publish conformance and limitations; the portal presents supported profiles and migration state through one catalog.

impacts.effect: The platform portfolio becomes explicitly federated around shared foundations and contracts rather than one giant implementation.
A specialist or acquired platform can adopt shared identity, delivery, telemetry, and catalog contracts without immediate replacement.
Conformance profiles make adoption incremental and gaps governable.
Foundation reuse is measurable across multiple provider implementations rather than one central stack.
Becomes a portfolio control plane and experience layer over several conforming delivery foundations.
Defines provider-neutral service intent, ownership, capabilities, controls, and operational obligations.
Shows profile, provider, conformance gaps, lifecycle, support route, and migration state in one catalog.
Resolves declared capabilities to cloud- and runtime-specific bindings through adapters.
Owns the common portfolio view and makes federation visible rather than hiding it as exceptions.
Raises provider-neutral orchestration and workload specification as a benchmark for the internal platform.
Presents federated stacks as explicit supported paths with capabilities, gaps, ownership, support, and migration state.

stressors.name: Coding agents create more services and production changes than humans can review
stressors.detection: Agent-authored pull requests, service-creation rate, review queues, machine credential use, change rollback patterns, and engineering workflow research.
stressors.attractor: Human review can no longer be the universal safety boundary; machine actors amplify both delivery and uncontrolled resource, dependency, security, and operational decisions.
stressors.businessReaction: Give agents bounded authority and machine-readable platform contracts, require evidence for controls, constrain cost and blast radius, stage changes, and preserve accountable human intervention.
stressors.residue: Model actor, principal, delegated purpose, budget, specification change, generated evidence, policy decision, rollout boundary, and revocation independently. The platform accepts intent only through the same versioned service contract and proves controls before progressively realizing it.

impacts.effect: The platform remains an everyday engineering tool when a software engineer delegates work to coding agents.
Shipping includes supervising machine-generated intent and evidence instead of manually reviewing every implementation detail.
Shows policy proof, provenance, cost, rollout scope, and intervention controls for agent-authored changes.
Delivery leverage includes safe agent-assisted throughput and its human supervision cost.
Extends software-supply-chain trust to machine actor, prompt or intent provenance, generated evidence, and delegated authority.
Produces bounded platform intent and evidence through supported contracts rather than uncontrolled shell access.
Evaluates machine identity, delegated purpose, cost, control evidence, and rollout limits as policy inputs.
Progressively promotes agent-authored changes under explicit blast-radius and revocation boundaries.
Owns the supported agent contract and its handoff to secure delivery controls.
Applies bounded agent authority, policy evidence, staged rollout, and intervention to the standard shipping path.
Makes machine-readable workload contracts and governed agent delivery a platform-orchestration benchmark.

stressors.name: A sovereignty rule requires code, builds, artifacts, telemetry, and operators to stay in one jurisdiction
stressors.detection: Legal and customer requirements, audit findings, cloud-region inventories, artifact lineage, support-access logs, and data-flow mapping.
stressors.attractor: Selecting a local runtime region is insufficient because development, control plane, identity, artifact distribution, telemetry, and incident support still cross the prohibited boundary.
stressors.businessReaction: Offer a declared sovereign delivery profile, prove every control and data flow, block incompatible dependencies, constrain support access, and make remaining capability differences explicit to product teams.
stressors.residue: Attach jurisdiction and operator constraints to the service specification and every supply-chain artifact. Capability resolution selects a complete location-compatible path for repository, build, registry, identity, runtime, telemetry, backup, and support; conformance evidence is generated from the realized graph.

impacts.effect: The normal platform path can make a jurisdiction-wide control boundary easier than parallel manual governance.
Control baseline includes the full software and operations chain, not only workload data residency.
Expresses location, operator, dependency, evidence, and exception constraints as a reusable profile.
Control coverage can be measured across the realized end-to-end service graph.
Provides a sovereign supply-chain profile with verifiable artifact and operator lineage.
Carries source, builder, dependency, jurisdiction, signature, and promotion evidence with every artifact.
Enforces eligible human and machine operators, access paths, secrets, and jurisdiction boundaries.
Realizes location-compatible telemetry and support access without leaking through a global default.
Owns the reusable sovereign identity and operator boundary with policy and runtime teams.
Turns sovereignty into a reusable delivery profile with explicit compatible paths, evidence, gaps, and exceptions.
Makes end-to-end sovereign conformance visible as a service-governance benchmark.

stressors.name: The company's highest-value product cannot run on containers or the preferred cloud
stressors.detection: Portfolio investment review, product architecture, mainframe and edge constraints, migration experiments, operating cost, and customer commitments.
stressors.attractor: The platform's most strategically important customer is classified as unsupported, so it either rebuilds parallel delivery plumbing or avoids the platform and weakens its organizational mandate.
stressors.businessReaction: Define the product's essential platform jobs, support a bounded non-standard runtime profile, reuse every compatible foundation, and make the cost and exceptions visible instead of pretending full conformity.
stressors.residue: Split golden paths into composable capability profiles. Source control, ownership, policy, artifact evidence, release intent, telemetry, incident, and catalog contracts can be reused while a runtime adapter implements only the unavoidable host-specific realization.

impacts.effect: Senior engineers retain judgment by choosing the closest supported capability profile instead of a binary standard-or-exception path.
The paved road becomes a composition of reusable contracts with an explicit runtime-specific adapter.
Compares capability coverage, gaps, ownership, cost, and evidence before selecting a profile.
Escape-hatch use becomes structured capability-gap data rather than an undifferentiated failure metric.
Supports a portfolio of runtime profiles that share delivery and operational contracts.
Composes paths from independently versioned capabilities rather than one template tied to one runtime.
Defines integration contracts and runtime-specific adapters at the explicit boundary.
Owns profile composition and turns strategic exceptions into reusable platform knowledge.
Guides teams to the closest supported capability profile and makes unavoidable runtime gaps explicit.
Makes composable provider-neutral golden paths a benchmark for supporting heterogeneous runtimes.

stressors.name: A strategic customer requires the product to run inside the customer's own cloud account
stressors.detection: Enterprise sales requirements, security review, procurement terms, customer architecture, data-location constraints, and deployment pilot evidence.
stressors.attractor: The company no longer owns the runtime account or every operational control, yet must deliver, update, support, and prove the same product outcomes within the customer's boundary.
stressors.businessReaction: Select a supported customer-hosted profile, declare shared responsibilities, realize only eligible capabilities, preserve artifact and release evidence, and expose operational gaps before contracting.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: provider-neutral service intent realizes through the federated capability adapters, while sovereign location, operator, artifact, and telemetry policies constrain the customer-owned target and generate conformance evidence.

impacts.effect: A product team can onboard a customer-hosted deployment through a supported profile instead of bespoke setup.
Resolves the service specification into the customer's eligible account with explicit responsibility boundaries.
Onboarding time can include customer-hosted profiles while exposing external approval wait separately.
Can govern a customer-owned target through the same specification and conformance model.
Binds declared capabilities to resources in a customer-owned account through an eligible adapter.
Promotes signed artifacts with lineage across the organizational boundary.
Can launch the profile through existing federation and sovereignty contracts, focusing on customer enablement.
Demonstrates portable workload realization as an internal-platform strength in enterprise delivery.
Product engineering can offer customer-hosted delivery as a governed supported profile rather than a bespoke commitment.
Provisions and verifies an eligible environment inside the customer's account under explicit shared responsibility.

stressors.name: A vendor offers a turnkey developer platform below the internal team's reported run cost
stressors.detection: Executive cost reviews, vendor proposals, renewal events, team satisfaction research, shadow-platform adoption, and benchmarked onboarding and delivery outcomes.
stressors.attractor: The internal platform is judged as undifferentiated tooling overhead; feature counts and infrastructure activity cannot justify investment against a packaged alternative.
stressors.businessReaction: Expose true service outcomes and total migration boundaries, distinguish commodity components from company-specific leverage, replace where appropriate, and invest where product context, controls, integration, or operating knowledge compounds.
stressors.residue: Treat platform capabilities as replaceable portfolio components with explicit consumers, contracts, conformance, cost, adoption, flow outcomes, and switching boundaries. Experience telemetry connects each capability to customer jobs so build, buy, retire, and federate decisions do not depend on platform mythology.

impacts.effect: The platform's promise is evaluated through product-team outcomes and trusted integration, not ownership of every tool.
Friction and shared-foundation recovery data become evidence for build, buy, and replacement decisions.
Relates customer effort and delivery outcomes to the exact capabilities and providers involved.
Redirected engineering capacity is measured net of platform team cost, migration work, and retained bespoke effort.
Provides portfolio-level adoption, flow, reliability, support, cost, and capability outcome evidence.
Connects workflow friction and satisfaction to versioned platform capabilities and providers.
Reports full capability and consumer economics rather than only cloud infrastructure spend.
Owns credible portfolio economics and outcome evidence for build, buy, and retirement choices.
Turns commercial platform offerings into component-level benchmarks instead of an all-or-nothing threat.
Connects capability adoption, friction, delivery outcome, reliability, cost, and switching evidence for build-or-buy decisions.
